statement:
Count how many hits arrived in the **past five minutes** (300 seconds).

- `hit(timestamp)` — record one hit at that second
- `getHits(timestamp)` — how many hits landed in the window `(timestamp - 300, timestamp]`

Timestamps arrive in non-decreasing order, and several hits may share a second.

examples.explanation: At t=301 the window is (1, 301], so the hit at second 1 has just fallen out.

why.d: Checks a hit leaving the window exactly 300 seconds later.

examples.explanation: Three hits share second 10; by t=310 all of them are outside the window.

why.d: Checks several hits in one second.

followUp: What if hits arrive at a million per second, or timestamps come as fractions of a second? A queue grows with traffic; per-second buckets do not, but they need an integer second to index by.
hints: Hits older than 300 seconds can never matter again, so they can be dropped rather than counted around.
The window is a fixed 300 seconds. That bound means you can keep one bucket per second and reuse them in a ring, which makes both operations O(1) regardless of traffic.

waysToSolve.name: Queue of timestamps
waysToSolve.idea: Append each hit; on getHits drop timestamps at or before t − 300 from the front, then return the size.
waysToSolve.use: Low or moderate traffic; simplest to explain.

waysToSolve.name: 300 per-second buckets
waysToSolve.idea: Bucket t % 300 stores the second it holds and its count; reset it when a newer second lands there, and sum the buckets still inside the window.
waysToSolve.use: Heavy traffic: memory stays fixed however many hits arrive.

variants.title: Per-client rate limiter
variants.approach: Deque of accepted timestamps per client · O(n) amortised · O(clients · limit)
variants.statement:
Requests reach an API gateway as `requests[i] = [timestamp, clientId]`, in non-decreasing timestamp order. Decide each one as it arrives:

- **allow** it if that client has had fewer than `limit` **allowed** requests in the window `(timestamp - window, timestamp]`
- otherwise **reject** it — a rejected request does not count against the client

Return one boolean per request, in order. This is the hit counter asked per client, on every request, with the answer acted on.

examples.explanation: The fourth request finds three allowed ones in (−6, 4]. At 11 the window is (1, 11], so the request from time 1 has left and a slot is free.

why.d: Checks a request leaving the window exactly `window` seconds later, freeing a slot.

examples.explanation: Clients 1 and 2 each get two requests; client 1's third request in the same window is rejected.

why.d: Checks that each client has its own allowance.

hints: Only allowed requests matter, and only the ones still inside the window — older ones can be thrown away.
Keep a queue of allowed timestamps per client. Before deciding, pop from the front while the oldest is `<= timestamp - window`.
After trimming, the queue's length is the client's count. It never exceeds `limit`, so memory stays bounded per client.

solutions.name: Full History per Client
solutions.description: Store every allowed timestamp for each client and, on each request, count the ones still inside the window by scanning the whole history.
keyPoints: Rescans the history on each request

solutions.name: Deque per Client (Optimal)
solutions.description: Each client owns a queue of its allowed timestamps that are still inside the window, oldest first. On a request, drop the ones that have aged out; allow it if fewer than `limit` remain and push its timestamp.
keyPoints: Each timestamp pushed and popped once
A queue never holds more than `limit`

variants.title: Hits in any time range
variants.approach: Two binary searches per query · O(q log n) · O(1) extra
variants.statement:
`hits` is a log of hit timestamps in **non-decreasing** order (several hits may share a second). The window is no longer the last 300 seconds: each `queries[j] = [start, end]` asks how many hits have `start <= timestamp <= end`.

Return the counts, one per query, in query order.

examples.explanation: [1, 2] holds 1, 2, 2; [2, 5] holds 2, 2, 5; nothing lies in [6, 8]; [0, 100] holds all five.

why.d: Checks duplicate hits counted separately and a range between hits.

examples.explanation: No hits were logged, so every range is empty.

why.d: Checks an empty `hits` list.

hints: In a sorted log, the hits inside `[start, end]` are one contiguous run.
Binary search for the first hit `>= start` and the first hit `> end`; the count is the difference of the two positions.

solutions.name: Scan Every Hit per Query
solutions.description: For each query, walk the whole log and count the hits inside the range. It ignores the sort order entirely.
keyPoints: Fine for a handful of queries

solutions.name: Two Binary Searches (Optimal)
solutions.description: The hits in `[start, end]` form one contiguous run of the sorted log. The first index with a hit `>= start` is where it begins, the first index with a hit `> end` is just past where it ends, and their difference is the count.

variants.title: Busiest window
variants.approach: Two pointers over the sorted log · O(n) · O(1)
variants.statement:
`hits` is a whole day's log of hit timestamps in **non-decreasing** order. A window of length `window` ending at second `s` covers `(s - window, s]` — the same shape `getHits` uses.

Return the **largest number of hits** any such window contains, or `0` when the log is empty. Capacity planning wants this peak, not the current value.

examples.explanation: The window (0, 300] holds 1, 2, 3 and 300; the windows ending at 301, 302 and 303 also hold four.

why.d: Checks a log where the busiest windows sit on both sides of a 300-second boundary.

examples.explanation: An empty log has no busy window at all.

why.d: Checks an empty `hits` list: the answer is 0.

hints: A window can slide right until its end touches a hit without losing anything, so only windows ending on a hit matter.
Fix the right end at each hit and move a left pointer forward while `hits[left] <= hits[right] - window`.
Neither pointer ever moves back, so the whole sweep is linear.

solutions.name: Count Back from Every Hit
solutions.description: For each hit, walk backwards through the log counting the hits inside the window that ends there, and keep the largest count.

complexity.time: O(n · k), k = hits per window

keyPoints: Only windows ending on a hit

solutions.name: Two Pointers (Optimal)
solutions.description: Sweep the right pointer across the sorted log; for each hit, advance the left pointer past hits that are too old for the window ending there. The window size `right - left + 1` is a candidate for the peak.
keyPoints: Windows ending on a hit suffice
Each hit enters and leaves once

variantApproach: 300 per-second buckets · O(1) hit, O(300) getHits · O(300)

solutions.name: Queue of Timestamps
solutions.description: Keep every hit's timestamp in arrival order. Timestamps never go backwards, so expired hits are always at the front: pop them on each getHits and the queue's size is the answer.
keyPoints: Expired hits sit at the front
Each hit is removed at most once

solutions.name: Circular Buffer of 300 Buckets (Optimal)
solutions.description: One bucket per second of the window, indexed by `timestamp % 300`. Each bucket remembers which second it holds; when a hit lands on a bucket holding an older second, reset it first. getHits adds up the buckets whose second is still within 300 of now.
keyPoints: Store the second with each bucket to detect stale data
Needs integer seconds to index by
